PETE: But will it last? Our written case measured investments alone: 33%. The fairer test is what a sensible family would do: sell the business when Carmen retires, keep the flat, and sell it only if they must. Across 10,000 simulated markets, in 51% they must. In a typical one, Carmen, at 83 and on her own, sells the home where they raised Ryan and Chloe. By 86 the money has run out again, and the wealth meant for their children pays the bills: of HK$24.4 million, just HK$2.3M is left to them. [Notes: Their own way: the business sold when Carmen retires; the flat kept and swapped for a HK$7M one only when the money runs out; the full budget after a death; the Flexi plan for life; equities 6% a year, inflation 2.5%, as in the written case. "Usually on her own": Adrian dies at 84 on the case's life expectancy, when Carmen is 79; she is alone in 83% of the forced sales. Even after the sale, the money lasts to 89 in only 62%. Why not a reverse mortgage at 83? It would let Carmen stay, but HKMC's fixed payout doesn't keep up with her bills and premiums: in Fahtai's test (HKMC's March 2026 table) the money lasts to 89 less often than selling, and the loan eats into what Ryan and Chloe inherit. Why it runs out (off the slide since 24 Oct; slides 6 and 7 fix each): 61% of their wealth, the home and the business, pays nothing until sold; HK$375K a year of medical premiums sit outside their budget.]

PETE: They asked for a plan that's innovative yet prudent. Our answer: five calls. Insure the income, not the life. Put the home and the business to work, on their terms. Fix the cost the budget ignores. Give each person a plan of their own. And make room for their values and Ryan's crypto, with guardrails. Done their own way, the money lasts to Carmen's 89 in 62%; the five calls lift it to 97%, and the home becomes their choice, not their last resort. Lookbua.

LOOKBUA: Thanks, Pete. Call one: insure the income, not the life. Neither parent has disability cover: if one couldn't work, their pay would stop. So disability cover comes first, 65% of pay until they retire; then critical illness, medical cover of their own, and a term-life top-up. About HK$100K a year, 14% of their surplus. Term, because the need ends at retirement. And within three months: wills, a guardian for Chloe, powers of attorney, and a buy-sell agreement so her business survives her. Fahtai. [Notes: Ryan: about HK$900 a year, term life only. On average the covers cost about HK$114K a year until each retires. Why term, not more whole life (whole life mostly buys savings they already hold); individual medical cover bought before group cover ends at 65 and 62.]

FAHTAI: Thanks, Lookbua. Call two: the home and the business will pay for their retirement either way. The question is when, and on whose terms. At 65 they choose: stay, with a reverse mortgage paying HK$230K a year for life, or downsize. The business is sold in stages to her co-founder and managers; we count only HK$3 million of its five. A survivor plans on 70%, and the MPF buys annuities. Four decisions, taken now: 83%, not 62%. [Notes: more shares instead? 80% in shares reaches only 43%, with a worst year of −24%, and breaks Adrian's low-to-medium profile. The annuities: HK$161K and HK$107K a year, single life; last on purpose, insurance for the worst markets. By 2039 guaranteed income covers 116% of essential bills; after Adrian's death 72%, so never "for life". Even if the business never sells, 66%. Stay or move keeps the odds at 83% either way; moving leaves more to the children. The annuities are HKMC's, bought at Adrian's 65 and Carmen's 62. If Adrian died soon after buying, the family wouldn't lose the money: HKMC pays the premium less what has been received as a lump sum, or keeps paying until 105% is returned (HKMC Annuity Plan brochure, April 2024); single life only, so one policy each. Why the rise isn't only the assets: about half of it is the survivor planning on 70%; even if their own way also cut her budget, deciding the home, business and MPF now still adds about ten points (Fahtai's model check, 23 Oct). HK$230K matches a joint loan with Carmen as the younger borrower: don't call it conservative.]

FAHTAI: Call three: the cost their budget leaves out. Kept on Flexi for life, medical premiums climb to HK$375K a year. So at Adrian's 75 they review the tier: the Standard plan costs about a third as much. And from 2039, two spending rules: no raise for inflation after a year markets fall, and a 10% trim only if they draw on savings too fast; essentials are never cut. Remember that future? Now the money lasts to 89, and the home stays theirs. The odds: 97% with the review, almost every future with the rules. Win. [Notes: in this future the four decisions alone leave HK$0.6M of savings at 89, under a year of spending; the review and the rules keep the rest (the lighter band). "Too fast": withdrawals 20% above their starting rate; spending rises back 10% when they run 20% below it, never above the budget. Cut the budget now instead? The problem arrives after 2047, so the decision waits until then. Why does the plan's total sit below their own way until about 2053? Part of the savings buys the annuities, and the home's value is drawn as income from 2037: the plan trades a peak for a floor, and then keeps going where their own way runs out. The home: worth less on the chart because the reverse-mortgage loan grows against it; it is still theirs, and they still live there. "19 futures out of 20": HK$382K is the 5th percentile of each future's leanest year, in today's money, with the rules; HK$111K without them. The switch is guaranteed: under the VHIS rules every Flexi policyholder can move to the insurer's Standard Plan at renewal without new medical checks, at any age (VHIS Code of Practice s.2.11; VHIS FAQ Q30, 25 Sep 2025); exclusions from the original policy stay, and no new ones can be added.]

WIN: Call five: values and innovation, with guardrails. Carmen asked for 20 to 25% in ESG. We reach 25%, up from 11%, in SFC-listed funds that must pass two ratings. Crypto isn't yes or no, it's sized per person. Adrian holds none; Carmen up to 2%, through an ETF; Ryan keeps his HK$500K but adds nothing new, so its share falls from 74% of his wealth to 20% by 35. Lookbua. [Notes: Off the slide since 25 Oct, said here if asked: the ratings are MSCI ESG A or better and Sustainalytics risk below 20, a downgrade replaced within three months; Adrian's tokenised money fund counts as cash; Chloe holds none while she studies; crypto only with no lending or leverage. The 25% replaces like for like (the global equity core, part of the bonds, half of each MPF), so each parent's risk stays where Call 4 set it; no return premium is assumed. Two ratings because ESG raters agree far less than credit raters (correlation about 0.54 against 0.99, Berg, Kölbel and Rigobon 2022); green bond funds also check every bond against ICMA; a downgraded fund is replaced within three months. Crypto: a platform that loses its licence means a move to an ETF within 30 days; self-custody only with a key-recovery plan, so heirs can inherit it. If the MPF move can't be made, the family still holds about 20%. Ryan at 30: about 32%; a rally more than 10 points above his path is trimmed back. A 70% fall costs Carmen about HK$29K at her cap. The three funds (written case Figure 16): BOC-Prudential MSCI World ESG Index Fund HK$1.49M, Sun Life MPF Global Low Carbon Index Fund HK$0.84M, Allianz Green Bond HK$0.31M.]

LOOKBUA: Then we tried to break the plan. The hardest test: Adrian loses his job at 60. The four decisions alone last in 30% of futures; the full plan, 83%. Years of low returns, or high inflation with dearer medical care: 92% or better. And if Carmen lives to 95: 99%. [Notes: we compare decisions in the same markets, we don't forecast them (also in the footer). The risk register's defences (off the slide since 25 Oct, said here if asked; written case Figure 26): the business doesn't sell: a buy-sell agreement now, and the plan lasts without the sale; three risk appetites: one risk profile and one portfolio per person; crypto rules or licences change: licensed channels only, into an ETF within 30 days; greenwashing: two ESG ratings per equity fund, replaced within three months of a downgrade; model risk: we compare decisions in the same markets, we don't forecast.]

PETE: The legacy the case is named for: in the futures where Carmen had to sell, the plan leaves Ryan and Chloe HK$7.7M, not HK$2.3M. And if either parent dies early, the wills name a guardian for Chloe and hold each child's share in trust until 25, 30 and 35. Meanwhile, a scholarship in sustainable design joins Carmen's mission to Chloe's interest. [Notes: the MPF has no nominee, so it passes through the wills. Control, not tax: Hong Kong abolished estate duty in 2006, so the wills decide who receives what, and when. The staged trusts matter only if a parent dies early: at Carmen's 89 Ryan is 64 and Chloe 56, so the HK$7.7M passes outright. The plan leaves more than their own way in 97% of those futures; part of the gap is our advice on the survivor budget and the medical review.]
